text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice to lead the CIA into the 21st century, George Tenet, warned on Tuesday that unspecified "terrorists" were stepping up their capabilities worldwide, posing an "enormously high" threat to U.S. interests.

"They have a capability to move money and people and explosives," Tenet said at the end of a cordial first day of U.S. Senate confirmation hearings. "They want us not thinking about what they're going to do next."
"But the fact is that the activity worldwide at this moment in time is unprecedented. The threat to U.S. interests is enormously high," he told the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence.

Tenet, 44, did not spell out which groups he thought posed this threat to the United States, but described them as "fanatical." He has held the intelligence community's second-ranking post since July 1995 and has served as acting chief U.S. spymaster since John Deutch left in December after 20 months in the job.

In his opening statement, Tenet said that if confirmed he planned on "closing the door on the Cold War" to focus more sharply on transnational threats such as narcotraffickers, nuclear proliferation and terrorism.

But he said the United States "cannot afford complacency about the unfinished transformations under way in countries like China and Russia, as long as there is any question about their future direction or even the slightest doubt about the ultimate fate of the nuclear weapons they control."

"One of the things I've done in my 'hard-target' reviews is I've requested we go back and look at the Russian target because my concern was that we have shifted too much resources away from it," he said in reply to a question from Sen. Jon Kyl, Republican of Arizona.
He did not immediately spell out why he thought Russia might bear closer watching by U.S. intelligence.

But Committee Vice Chairman Bob Kerrey said he feared the United States was not dealing as "aggressively" as it should to prevent old Soviet ballistic missile technology or nuclear material from falling into the wrong hands.

Tenet said the people he described as terrorists "have every reason to continue doing what they're doing and I am quite concerned." Although the State Department said in an annual report last week that the number of "terrorist" attacks declined last year to the lowest level in 25 years, Tenet cautioned against complacency.

"Don't judge it by the number of incidents," he said in reply to a question from Kerrey, a Democrat from Nebraska. "Don't judge it by the number of casualties because it doesn't take much to get your attention all over again. And that's exactly where they want us."
In its annual report, the State Department branded the fundamentalist government of Iran as the chief state sponsor of what it called international terrorism.

Tenet told the committee that in the post-Cold War world U.S. spy agencies "must be able to adjust our collection posture quickly, draw more heavily on outside expertise and ensure that we are not caught unaware in parts of the world that move quickly from backwater to front burner."

The son of a Greek immigrant father and a mother who fled Albania, Tenet would be the fifth director of central intelligence in six years and the third to serve under Clinton. He grew up in the New York City borough of Queens, where he once cleaned tables at his parents' diner.
Clinton tapped Tenet for the chief spymaster job after a bruising fight with Senate Republicans over the abortive nomination of Anthony Lake, the president's first-term national security adviser.
Tenet is a former staff director of the Intelligence Committee who later became senior intelligence adviser on the White House National Security Council staff under Lake.
If confirmed, he would not only run the CIA but oversee the 12 other U.S. spy agencies that together employ about 80,000 people and spend about $30 billion a year.
